overview.title: Indexing with [UNK], and why text needs standardization
overview.main_topic: Completing the vocabulary lookup with an unknown-token fallback, then introducing text standardization (lowercasing, punctuation and accent removal, stemming/lemmatization)
overview.central_idea: A vocabulary lookup with a default of [UNK] = 0 lets us index any input, even unseen words. Superficial encoding differences (case, punctuation, accents, word forms) make near-identical sentences look completely different after indexing, so we standardize text before splitting; lowercasing and removing punctuation is the simplest widespread scheme.
overview.importance: It completes the first working tokenizer pipeline and introduces the third preprocessing stage, standardization, which the book formalizes on p.411 as Standardization -> Splitting -> Indexing.
learning_objectives: Trace the list comprehension vocabulary.get(word, 0) and derive the output [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8]
Explain the role of the [UNK] token for out-of-vocabulary terms
Explain why near-identical sentences can get very different indices without standardization
Apply lowercasing and punctuation removal to an example

summary:
The page completes the hand-built vocabulary from p.409 with `"over": 6, "dog": 7, ".": 8`, splits the full sentence with `split_words`, and indexes each word with `vocabulary.get(word, 0)`. The output is `[0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8]`.

The authors explain the special token **`[UNK]`** ("unknown"): it lets us index all input, even terms that only appear in test data. In the example, "lazy" is not in the vocabulary and maps to index 0. *Note (not in the book):* the **first** 0 has the same cause. `split_words` keeps "The" capitalized, while the vocabulary only has lowercase "the", so "The" is also unknown. That illustrates the next topic.

**Standardization.** The two sentences "sunset came. i was staring at the Mexico sky. Isnt nature splendid??" and "Sunset came; I stared at the México sky. Isn't nature splendid?" are almost identical, yet they would get very different indices: "i" vs. "I", "Mexico" vs. "México", "isnt" vs. "isn't", "staring" vs. "stared". A model does not know these equivalences a priori. Standardizing text is described as **a basic form of feature engineering** that erases encoding differences you don't want the model to deal with, and the authors note that search engines need the same thing.

The simplest widespread scheme is to **lowercase and remove punctuation**, which gives "sunset came i was staring at the mexico sky isnt nature splendid" and "sunset came i stared at the méxico sky isnt nature splendid". Removing accent marks would bring them even closer. Standardization used to be one of the most critical areas for improving performance: for decades NLP used regexes to map words to a common root ("tired" -> "tire", "trophies" -> "trophy"), called **stemming** or **lemmatization**. The sentence continues on p.411, which says that this kind of heavy standardization now tends to do more harm than good for large models.

paragraphs.excerpt: We introduce a special token called "[UNK]" to our vocabulary, which represents
paragraphs.what_it_says: The [UNK] token represents any token unknown to the vocabulary, so all input can be indexed, even terms that only occur in test data. In the example, "lazy" maps to [UNK] index 0 because it was not included in the vocabulary.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A vocabulary is built from training data and is finite, but test data can contain new words. Instead of crashing (a KeyError) or skipping them, the lookup falls back to a reserved index. In the code, that is the default argument of vocabulary.get(word, 0).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Every real tokenizer needs an out-of-vocabulary strategy. [UNK] is the simplest one, but it throws away information; p.414 points out that aggressive vocabulary limits send a lot of text to [UNK], which motivates subword tokenization.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The output [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8] contains two zeros. The book explains the second ("lazy"); the first is "The", which is unknown because the vocabulary is lowercase and split_words does not lowercase. Standardization (next paragraphs) fixes exactly that.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Splitting and indexing already go a long way toward a text preprocessing pipeline, but one more common manipulation is needed: standardization. Two example sentences are introduced.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The pipeline so far is split -> index. The authors are about to add a step before splitting that normalizes the text itself.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up the three-stage pipeline (standardize, split, index) shown as figure 14.1 on p.411.

paragraphs.excerpt: They are very similar—in fact, they are almost identical. Yet, if you
paragraphs.what_it_says: The two sentences are almost identical, but indexing them as described would give very different representations because "i" vs. "I", "Mexico" vs. "México" and "isnt" vs. "isn't" differ. A model doesn't know a priori that "i" and "I" are the same letter, that "é" is an accented "e", or that "staring" and "stared" are forms of the same verb. Standardizing text is a basic form of feature engineering that erases encoding differences you don't want your model to deal with, and search engines need it too.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Indices are exact-match identifiers: two strings that differ by one character get unrelated indices, so the model sees them as unrelated tokens and has to learn their equivalence from data, if it can. Standardization builds that equivalence into preprocessing, which shrinks the vocabulary and pools statistics across variants.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It names the trade-off: standardization is hand-written knowledge (feature engineering), which deep learning usually tries to minimize. The following text (pp.410-411) shows that the right amount depends on model size.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a search engine applies the same normalization to the query and the documents, so "México" matches "mexico"; this is the analogy the authors draw.

terminology.meaning: Hand-designing input transformations that make a learning problem easier.
Surface variations (case, accents, punctuation) that do not change meaning in the given context.

connections: p.411: for large modern models, most standardization is kept as light as possible.

paragraphs.excerpt: One simple and widespread standardization scheme is to convert to lowercase and
paragraphs.what_it_says: Lowercasing and removing punctuation is a simple, widespread scheme. Applied to the two sentences, it gives "sunset came i was staring at the mexico sky isnt nature splendid" and "sunset came i stared at the méxico sky isnt nature splendid".
paragraphs.what_it_means: After the scheme, only two differences remain: "was staring" vs. "stared" and "mexico" vs. "méxico". Case differences, ";" vs. ".", "??" vs. "?" and the apostrophe in "isn't" are all gone.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows concretely how much variation two cheap operations remove. CharTokenizer and WordTokenizer (pp.411-412) use only lowercasing.

terminology.meaning: Converting all characters to lowercase so that case variants share a token.

connections: p.411: Listing 14.1's standardize method is inputs.lower().

paragraphs.excerpt: Much closer already. We could get even closer if we removed accent
paragraphs.what_it_says: The lowercased, punctuation-free sentences are much closer, and removing accent marks on all characters would make them closer still.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Accent removal (e.g. é -> e) would make "méxico" and "mexico" identical, leaving only the verb-form difference.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Each standardization step removes a class of surface variation, but it can also remove meaning (in some languages accents distinguish words).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: accent stripping is commonly done with Unicode NFD decomposition followed by dropping combining marks.

terminology.meaning: Mapping accented characters to their base letter, e.g. "é" -> "e".

paragraphs.excerpt: There’s a lot you can do with standardization, and it used to
paragraphs.what_it_says: Standardization has many options and used to be among the most critical ways to improve model performance. For decades NLP used regular expressions to map words to a common root ("tired" -> "tire", "trophies" -> "trophy"), which is called stemming or lemmatization. The sentence continues with "But" onto p.411.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Stemming/lemmatization merges inflected forms (tense, plural) into one token so a small model with little data can pool evidence across "stared", "staring" and "stare". The "But" signals a reversal: p.411 says this harms today's larger models, because tense and plurality carry meaning.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It marks a historical shift: preprocessing that once added accuracy is now often avoided, a recurring theme of deep learning replacing feature engineering.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: strictly, stemming chops suffixes by rules (and may give non-words such as "trophi"), while lemmatization maps to a dictionary form using vocabulary and morphology ("trophies" -> "trophy"). The book groups them together.

terminology.meaning: Rule-based reduction of a word to a root by stripping affixes.
Mapping a word to its dictionary base form (lemma).

connections: p.411: "as models have grown more expressive, this type of standardization tends to do more harm than good."

concepts.name: Unknown token [UNK] / out-of-vocabulary handling
concepts.definition: A reserved vocabulary entry to which every token not in the vocabulary is mapped.
concepts.intuition: A catch-all bin for words the tokenizer has never seen.
concepts.technical: Implemented as the default in vocabulary.get(token, unk_id). Index 0 here. All OOV tokens become indistinguishable.
concepts.significance: Guarantees any input can be indexed, including test-only terms.
concepts.misconception: [UNK] does not preserve the word; information is lost, which is why subword tokenizers (p.414) try to avoid it.

concepts.name: Text standardization
concepts.definition: Text-to-text normalization that erases encoding differences you don't want the model to deal with; the book calls it a basic form of feature engineering.
concepts.intuition: Ironing out cosmetic differences so that the same word always looks the same.
concepts.technical: Typical operations: lowercasing, stripping punctuation, removing accents, Unicode normalization, stemming/lemmatization. Applied before splitting; reduces vocabulary size and pools token statistics.
concepts.significance: The first of the three preprocessing stages in figure 14.1 (p.411).
concepts.example: "Sunset came; I stared at the México sky." -> "sunset came i stared at the méxico sky"
concepts.misconception: More standardization is not always better: p.411 says heavy standardization harms modern large models because tense and plurality carry meaning.

concepts.name: Stemming / lemmatization
concepts.definition: Mapping words to a common root, traditionally with regular expressions, e.g. "tired" -> "tire", "trophies" -> "trophy".
concepts.intuition: Treat all forms of a word as one word.
concepts.technical: Stemming strips suffixes by rules; lemmatization uses morphology and a dictionary. Both reduce vocabulary size at the cost of grammatical information.
concepts.significance: Was a key performance lever in classical NLP; now mostly avoided for large models (p.411).
concepts.misconception: Not in the book: the two terms are not identical; stemming can produce non-words, while lemmatization produces dictionary forms.

concepts.name: Indexing with a vocabulary lookup
concepts.definition: Mapping each token to its vocabulary index, with [UNK] as the default.
concepts.intuition: Look each word up in the dictionary; if it is missing, write 0.
concepts.technical: [vocabulary.get(word, 0) for word in words], an O(n) list comprehension over the tokens.
concepts.significance: Produces the integer sequence models consume.
concepts.misconception: Lookups are exact string matches: case and accents matter unless the text is standardized.

deeper.title: Applying the standardization scheme in code
deeper.body:
An illustrative implementation (not from the book):

```python
import re, unicodedata
def standardize(text, strip_accents=False):
    text = text.lower()
    text = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", "", text)      # drop punctuation
    if strip_accents:
        text = "".join(c for c in unicodedata.normalize("NFD", text)
                       if unicodedata.category(c) != "Mn")
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

standardize("Sunset came; I stared at the México sky. Isn't nature splendid?")
# 'sunset came i stared at the méxico sky isnt nature splendid'
```

With `strip_accents=True`, "méxico" becomes "mexico", which is the "even closer" step the book mentions.

deeper.title: Standardization as a bias you build in
deeper.body: Each standardization rule is an assumption: "case never matters", "punctuation never matters", "tense never matters". With little data and small models, these assumptions help by pooling evidence. With huge data and expressive models, the model can learn which differences matter, and a wrong assumption (e.g. "US" vs. "us", or tense in "I will go" vs. "I went") costs accuracy. That is the reversal p.411 describes.

misconceptions.correction: The capitalized "The" also maps to 0 because the vocabulary contains only lowercase "the" and split_words does not lowercase.

misconceptions.claim: A model will automatically treat "I" and "i" or "México" and "Mexico" as the same.
misconceptions.correction: After indexing, they are different integers; the model doesn't know a priori that they are equivalent unless standardization merges them or it learns it from data.

misconceptions.claim: Stemming and heavy standardization always improve NLP models.
misconceptions.correction: They used to be critical, but p.411 says that for today's larger models they tend to do more harm than good.

questions.question: Why is the FIRST element of [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8] equal to 0?
options: "The" is a stop word removed by split_words
"The" is capitalized and the vocabulary only contains lowercase "the"
Indices always start at 0 for the first token
questions.answer: "The" is capitalized and the vocabulary only contains lowercase "the"
questions.explanation: split_words preserves case, and vocabulary.get("The", 0) misses, so it returns the default 0. split_words removes nothing but whitespace; indices are lookups, not positions; and [UNK] is a vocabulary entry, not the word "The".

questions.question: What problem does the [UNK] token solve?
questions.answer: It lets us index all input, even terms not in the vocabulary (e.g. ones that only occur in test data), by mapping them to a reserved index.
questions.explanation: The book: "This way, we can index all input we come across, even if some terms only occur in our test data."

questions.question: Why do the two "sunset" sentences end up with very different index sequences without standardization?
questions.answer: Indexing is exact string matching: "i"/"I", "Mexico"/"México", "isnt"/"isn't" and "staring"/"stared" are different strings and get different (or unknown) indices, and the model doesn't know a priori that they are equivalent.
questions.explanation: This is the argument in the paragraph "They are very similar...".

questions.question: After lowercasing and punctuation removal, which difference between the two sentences remains?
questions.explanation: Lowercasing removes case differences and punctuation removal removes the apostrophe and question marks; the accent survives, which is why the book says removing accent marks would bring them even closer.

questions.question: What is stemming or lemmatization, and give the book's examples.
questions.answer: Mapping words to a common root, traditionally with regular expressions: "tired" -> "tire", "trophies" -> "trophy".
questions.explanation: Defined in the last paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Why do the authors call standardization "a basic form of feature engineering"?
questions.answer: Because it is a hand-designed transformation of the input that builds in human knowledge (case or accents don't matter) to make learning easier, instead of letting the model learn it.
questions.explanation: Feature engineering means hand-crafting input transformations; standardization erases differences "you don't want your model to have to deal with."

questions.question: Modify the indexing code mentally so that the output has only one 0. What single change suffices?
questions.answer: Lowercase the input before splitting (e.g. split_words(text.lower())), so that "The" becomes "the" -> 1; only "lazy" remains unknown.
questions.explanation: This is exactly what CharTokenizer/WordTokenizer's standardize step does on pp.411-412.
